text:
Every vehicle crossing a suspension bridge, along with the immense weight of the roadway itself, begins its path to the earth at the bridge deck. The deck bears both live loads, such as traffic and wind pressure, and dead loads, consisting of the permanent structural materials of the span. Because a simple slab would bend excessively under concentrated weights, the deck is integrated into a continuous stiffening truss or aerodynamic box girder. This stiffening structure spreads localized forces across a wider section, preventing sharp deflections and resisting the twisting effects of crosswinds. Along the edges of the deck, steel sockets attach the roadway to vertical wire ropes known as suspenders or hangers. Instead of propping the roadway from below, these suspenders pull upward, converting the downward push of the deck and its traffic into tension traveling up the cables.

At their upper ends, the suspenders clamp onto the sweeping main cables that define a suspension bridge. Each main cable is formed from thousands of high-strength steel wires bundled tightly together. As the suspenders tug downward at regular intervals, the main cables gather those vertical forces into continuous, massive tension running along their length. Under the weight of the deck, the cables settle into a parabolic curve, a geometric shape that avoids bending stresses and lets the steel work purely in tension. Because flexible cables cannot support compression, they respond to the suspended load by pulling taut between their elevated supports, channeling the accumulated forces simultaneously toward the bridge towers and outward toward the shorelines.

Where the main cables pass over the tops of the tall towers, they rest in heavy steel saddles that distribute pressure evenly and permit slight movements from shifting traffic or temperature changes. As the main span pulls down on one side of the saddle and the backstay pulls down on the other, their downward-sloping angles create an enormous net vertical force pressing straight down. The towers absorb this force and carry it down through their shafts as pure compression. Built of reinforced concrete or steel, the towers function as giant columns transferring the combined weight of the roadway, traffic, and cables down into deep foundations, typically caissons or piers seated firmly on bedrock beneath the water or ground, grounding the vertical portion of the load.

The immense horizontal tension of the main cables, however, must also be anchored so the towers are not pulled inward. Beyond the tower saddles, the cables descend toward land as backstays and terminate inside massive anchorages at each end of the bridge. Within an anchorage, each main cable splays into individual strands fastened to heavy steel bars embedded in enormous concrete blocks or locked directly into solid bedrock. Relying on sheer weight and friction against the surrounding earth, these anchorages counteract the relentless inward and upward tug of the cables. Through this coordinated chain of compression and tension, every load applied to the deck travels through the suspenders, cables, towers, and anchorages into the ground.
